points.label: Training adjusts the model
points.description: The learner states that training is the phase where the model's parameters are adjusted using labeled data, typically by measuring errors on examples and updating parameters to reduce those errors.

points.label: Inference uses the frozen model
points.description: The learner states that inference (prediction) is the phase where the already-trained model, with parameters held fixed, is applied to new inputs to produce outputs; no learning happens during inference.

points.label: Different requirements per phase
points.description: The learner explains at least one practical difference between the phases: training needs labeled data and is computationally expensive and done ahead of time, while inference needs only features, is comparatively cheap per input, and happens each time the model is used.

misconceptions.summary: A deployed model keeps learning from every prediction it makes.
misconceptions.belief: My understanding is that once a model is deployed, every prediction it makes is another learning opportunity, so it keeps improving automatically the more people use it.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Apps really do seem to get better over time, and 'machine learning' sounds like something that should keep learning whenever it runs.
misconceptions.fallback_line: It's called machine learning, and popular apps clearly improve as more people use them — so every prediction a deployed model makes teaches it something new.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that a standard deployed model does not update itself during inference; its parameters stay fixed until someone retrains it, so using the model more does not make it smarter on its own.

misconceptions.summary: Training and inference are the same computation, just run at different times.
misconceptions.belief: I think training and inference run the exact same computation — the model processes inputs and produces outputs either way, and we just call it different names depending on when it happens.
misconceptions.why_plausible: In both phases the same model takes inputs and produces outputs, so the underlying computation looks identical from the outside.
misconceptions.fallback_line: In both training and inference the model takes an input and produces an output, so they're the same computation — we just run it at different times with different data.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that training involves an extra loop absent at inference: computing errors against known labels and updating parameters (e.g. via gradient descent), whereas inference is a single forward pass from input to output with no labels and no updates.

beginner: So when I use a translation app on my phone, is that training or inference? What is the app actually doing?
Why does training take days on big computers but getting a prediction takes less than a second?
confident: Every time users interact with a model, it automatically learns from them — that's why apps get better over time.
You need labels at inference time too, otherwise the model couldn't check whether it's right.
skeptic: If the model is frozen after training, doesn't it become stale as soon as the world changes? What's the point of deploying something that stops learning?
How can we trust inference on inputs the training data never covered? The freeze seems like it locks in blind spots forever.
